items.title: Your core temperature varies by less than 1 degree all day
items.claim: Air temperature swings by 30 degrees C between Australian outback day and night. Sahara desert: 50 C day, 0 C night. Yet healthy human core temperature stays at 36.5-37.5 C across these extremes. We are walking thermostats.
items.prompt: How does the body hold core temperature constant?

options.text: The skin acts as insulation only

Negative feedback through the hypothalamus: sensors monitor core temperature; effectors include sweating (cooling), vasodilation/vasoconstriction (heat dump or retention), shivering (heat production), and behavioural responses (seek shade, put on clothes)
Body heat is generated constantly at the same rate

items.reveal:
The preoptic area of the hypothalamus contains warm-sensitive and cold-sensitive neurons. They integrate skin temperature (peripheral) and blood temperature (core) and adjust effector outputs.

When too hot: blood vessels in skin dilate; sweat glands release ~0.5-1.5 L/hour (up to 3 L/hour in heat-acclimated athletes); behaviour (seek shade).

When too cold: skin vessels constrict; shivering (involuntary skeletal muscle activity, heat output up to 5x resting); brown fat thermogenesis (less in adults); piloerection (goose bumps — useless on hairless humans but works in furred mammals); behaviour (seek shelter).

Fever is a deliberately raised set-point — the hypothalamus is told (by pyrogens) that 38.5 C is the new target. Your body now defends 38.5 the way it usually defends 37.

Heatstroke: thermoregulation fails at core temperatures above ~40 C. Mortality rises rapidly. Conversely, deep hypothermia (<30 C) shuts down cardiac function — but has been used surgically to extend safe ischemia times.

The set-point isn't constant: circadian variation (~0.5 C lower at night), menstrual cycle (~0.3 C higher post-ovulation), age-related decline in regulation precision.
items.why: Homeostasis is usually drawn as a circle on a board. It's an integration of dozens of mechanisms across the whole body — and breaks down in fascinating ways (fever, heatstroke, hypothermia) when stressed.

items.title: Babies have a special fat that wastes energy as heat — on purpose
items.claim: Brown adipose tissue, found in newborns and hibernating mammals, contains mitochondria packed with a protein (UCP1) that lets protons leak back across the inner membrane WITHOUT making ATP. The energy is dissipated as pure heat.
items.prompt: Why deliberately uncouple respiration from ATP synthesis?

options.text: It's a mistake the body cannot fix
Newborns and small mammals lose heat fast (high surface area to volume ratio). Brown fat lets them generate large amounts of heat on demand without shivering — burning fat directly to warmth

items.reveal:
In ordinary mitochondria, the electron transport chain pumps protons OUT; ATP synthase lets them back IN, capturing the energy as ATP.

In brown adipose tissue, the protein UCP1 (uncoupling protein 1, also called thermogenin) provides an alternative route for protons to flow back in — bypassing ATP synthase. The proton gradient still forms; the energy still flows; but it dissipates as heat rather than ATP.

Brown fat is brown because it's packed with mitochondria (iron-rich cytochromes). It's especially abundant in newborn humans (around the neck and shoulder blades) and in hibernating mammals (which use it to wake from torpor).

Adults retain some brown fat, more in lean people; PET-CT scans light it up. There's active research into pharmacologically activating brown fat as an anti-obesity strategy.

The drug DNP (2,4-dinitrophenol) chemically uncouples mitochondria. It does cause weight loss — but also fatal hyperthermia. It's been banned for human use for nearly a century, though it still kills bodybuilders occasionally.
items.why: Inefficiency seems like a flaw. The body uses controlled mitochondrial inefficiency as a thermostat — and biotech is trying to weaponise it against obesity.

items.title: Your kidneys filter 180 litres of blood plasma every day
items.claim: Each kidney has about a million nephrons. Together they filter 125 ml of plasma per minute — 180 litres per day. Your final urine output is 1 to 2 litres. The kidneys reabsorb 99% of what they filter.
items.prompt: Why filter so much only to put it back?

options.text: Bulk filtration is the only way to expose all blood-borne solutes to selective reabsorption; the kidney keeps what's needed (glucose, salts, amino acids, water) and lets the rest go — fine selectivity requires high throughput
The body has extra water to spare

items.reveal:
The glomerulus is a knot of capillaries inside a Bowman's capsule. Blood pressure forces plasma (minus proteins and cells) through a selective barrier into the nephron tubule.

Flow rates: glomerular filtration rate (GFR) ~120-125 ml/min in healthy adults. Total renal blood flow ~1.2 L/min — about 20-25% of cardiac output. The kidneys take a major share of the circulation for their mass.

The filtrate then passes through the tubules. Proximal tubule reabsorbs glucose, amino acids, most salts, water. Loop of Henle sets up an osmotic gradient. Distal tubule fine-tunes. Collecting duct adjusts water under ADH (antidiuretic hormone).

Result: 180 L filtered, 178.5 L returned to blood, 1.5 L excreted as urine.

GFR drops with age (~1% per year after 40), kidney disease, dehydration. Maintaining it is why drinking water matters — and why drugs that affect kidney function require careful monitoring.
items.why: Filtration that throws everything out and re-claims most of it sounds wasteful. It's the simplest design that ensures any potentially harmful blood-borne molecule eventually leaves the body.
